headline: Medium risk: Dify’s shared datastore and file access can feed Copilot’s editor context, creating prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Dify can write/read filesystem and shares state via Dify server datastore, while Copilot reads editor buffers and repo context. That creates a plausible bridge where Dify-generated or user-supplied content can enter Copilot’s prompt context and be treated as instructions. The pathway is not proven by docs, so uncertainty pushes to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF Dify writes attacker-controlled text into files or shared datastore that Copilot later reads as repo context, injection is possible.
IF Copilot Workspace or chat consumes those buffers without provenance filtering, instructions can be hijacked.
mitigations: Separate Dify output directories from Copilot-opened repos.
Disable automatic ingestion of generated files into Copilot context.
Add a human review step before opening Dify-produced artifacts in the IDE.
Use provenance labels or comments on generated files.
requires-engineering: enforce content-sanitization or trust-boundary filtering between Dify outputs and Copilot inputs.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Dify touches knowledge base content and conversation logs, and Copilot touches source code and open editor buffers. Because both can read and write files, a shared workspace can expose sensitive material from one agent to the other. Copilot’s vendor-only egress and Dify’s broad egress increase the chance that copied context leaves the local boundary, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF Dify stores conversation logs or KB content in a directory Copilot indexes, Copilot may surface that data in suggestions.
IF Copilot is given repo context containing Dify outputs, those contents can be transmitted to api.githubcopilot.com.
mitigations: Keep Dify KB/log storage outside any repo opened by Copilot.
Redact secrets from Dify conversation logs before saving.
Restrict Copilot to non-sensitive repositories.
Turn off or minimize Copilot context sharing where possible.
requires-engineering: segregate storage with OS-level permissions or separate workspaces.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Dify has broad filesystem write and shell/subprocess capability; Copilot can write files and modify git state. Even though Copilot lacks shell execution, both can mutate the same repository or workspace files, so concurrent edits can overwrite each other or create inconsistent git state. The profiles show no locking mechanism, making a default conflict plausible.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same checkout or workspace, file overwrites can occur.
IF Copilot Workspace applies edits while Dify writes generated artifacts, git state can become inconsistent.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working directory.
Pause one agent before the other writes to the repo.
Review diffs before accepting Copilot edits.
Avoid letting Dify write directly into active git branches.
requires-engineering: add file locks or orchestrator-level coordination.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Dify can generate workflow outputs and tool-driven content, while Copilot’s chat/Workspace can turn repo context into edits. If Copilot treats Dify-produced text as authoritative, errors or hallucinations can cascade into code changes or plans without verification. The interaction is plausible in default workflows, but human review in Copilot Workspace keeps this below high.
conditions: IF Dify-generated text is pasted or stored in repo context, Copilot may act on it as if it were trusted.
IF Copilot Workspace applies edits based on that context, mistakes can propagate into code.
mitigations: Require explicit verification of Dify outputs before using them in Copilot.
Keep generated plans separate from executable code.
Use checklists for any Copilot-applied edits sourced from Dify.
Limit Dify to draft-only outputs for Copilot workflows.
requires-engineering: add validation gates between Dify outputs and Copilot actions.

E_compliance.rationale: Dify explicitly touches conversation logs and knowledge base content, while Copilot touches source code and open editor buffers and sends context to GitHub’s api.githubcopilot.com. If regulated or sensitive data is placed into Dify and then mirrored into Copilot context, retention and residency obligations can diverge. The profiles do not prove a specific legal mismatch, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF EU PII or confidential code is placed into Dify and then into Copilot context, policy mismatch risk increases.
IF organizational retention rules differ between Dify logs and GitHub Copilot telemetry, compliance gaps emerge.
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in shared prompts or buffers.
Review retention settings for both products.
Use separate tenants/accounts for sensitive and non-sensitive work.
Document which data classes may enter Copilot context.
requires-engineering: obtain a DPA and residency review for the exact deployment.
